objective: Compare retained original ASCII letters/digits without introducing content through Unicode lowercasing.

relevanceRationale.presentDay: Two pointers and explicit character classification remain current text-processing basics.
relevanceRationale.practicalUtility: Comparing normalized retained content is practical string work.
relevanceRationale.transferable: Classification order, case semantics and empty filtering transfer to validators.
relevanceRationale.audienceFit: An explicit ASCII contract fits the original regex/character-code teaching approach.
relevanceRationale.riskOutcome: Lowercasing Unicode first can turn ignored text into new ASCII letters and change the answer.

defects: The brief said letters/digits generally while the reference used an ASCII class.
Junior/senior lowercased globally before filtering, unlike the reference’s original-character classification.
No original examples exercised Kelvin-sign/dotted-I conversion into ASCII content.
rationale: Explicitly define ASCII content, original-character classification before ASCII lowercasing, ignored other UTF-16 units and no Unicode normalization/full-language folding. Repair junior’s per-character classification and senior’s filter-before-lowercase order; keep the correct pointer reference. One visible Kelvin-sign example and three hidden assertions cover dotted-I/Kelvin/non-ASCII letters/digits, emoji/combining marks, ASCII digits/case/empty punctuation, booleans and1000-unit bounds. An independent character-code pointer alternative passes9331 native short-text comparisons against an ASCII-cleaned oracle. Pointer storage is O(1); cleaned-copy boards remain behaviorally valid O(n)-time alternatives with explicitly O(n) memory, as allowed by the brief’s conditional space goal. No space-based XP penalty or TypeScript tests are introduced.
